ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
The figure below shows a ring made of six small sections which you are to paint on a wall. You have four paint colors available and will paint each of the six sections a solid color. Find the number of ways you can choose to paint each of the six sections if no two adjacent section can be painted with the same color.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The attached figure shows an annular ring divided by radial line segments into exactly six wedge-like sections arranged all the way around the ring, forming a closed loop of six adjacent regions. Reasoning: Since each of the six sections is adjacent to the two neighboring sections around the ring, the adjacency graph is a 6-cycle. There are 4 available colors, and adjacent sections cannot have the same color. For a cycle with n vertices and k colors, the number of proper colorings is (k-1)^n + (-1)^n(k-1). Substituting n = 6 and k = 4 gives (4-1)^6 + (-1)^6(4-1) = 3^6 + 3 = 729 + 3 = 732.

method.method_draft: First describe the image as six labeled positions around a ring, numbered 1 through 6 in cyclic order, with section 6 adjacent back to section 1. From the text, use 4 colors and the rule that neighboring positions cannot match. Count colorings of the linear chain of six first, then enforce the closing condition. Choose a color for section 1 in 4 ways. For sections 2 through 6, there are 3 choices each if only linear adjacency is considered, giving 4·3^5 preliminary colorings. Among these, subtract the colorings where section 6 accidentally equals section 1. To count those bad cases, fix section 1 and section 6 to the same color and properly color the intervening path sections 2–5 with endpoint restrictions; equivalently use a recurrence for paths tracking whether the current section equals the first color. This gives 183 bad colorings total, so the valid cyclic count is 4·3^5−183=732.
